title: What Miles Davis Taught Herbie Hancock: In Music, as in Life, There Are No Mistakes, Just Chances to Improvise
description:
in Life, Music |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One of my favorite Bri­an Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strat­e­gy
body:
in Life, Music |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

One of my favorite Bri­an Eno quotes, or rather one that became an Oblique Strat­e­gy, is “Hon­or Your Mis­take as a Hid­den Inten­tion.” (Or to be pedan­tic, the orig­i­nal ver­sion was “Hon­or Thy Error…”).
As a teenag­er grow­ing up and try­ing to make art (at that time music and comics) there was no advice more free­ing. It was the oppo­site of what I thought I knew: mis­takes were shame­ful, the sign of an ama­teur or of the lack of prac­tice. But the more art I made, the more I ref­er­enced Eno’s idea, and the more I read and lis­tened, the more I real­ized it wasn’t just Eno.
The Bea­t­les left in an alarm clock meant for the musi­cians on “A Day in the Life” and the sound of emp­ty booze bot­tles vibrat­ing on a speak­er was left in at the end of “Long Long Long” (along with tons more). The Beast­ie Boys left in a jump­ing nee­dle intend­ed for a smooth scratch on “The Sounds of Sci­ence.” Radio­head left in Jon­ny Greenwood’s warm-up chord that became essen­tial to “Creep.” (There’s a whole Red­dit thread devot­ed to these mis­takes if you choose to go down the rab­bit hole.)
But those exam­ples relate to the record­ing process of rock music. What about jazz? Sure­ly there are “wrong” notes when it comes to play­ing, espe­cial­ly if you’re not the soloist.
In this very short video based around an inter­view with pianist Her­bie Han­cock, the mas­ter impro­vis­er Miles Davis hon­ored Hancock’s mis­take as a hid­den inten­tion by play­ing along with it. It’s both a sur­pris­ing look into the arcane world of jazz impro­vi­sa­tion and a reveal­ing anec­dote of Davis, usu­al­ly known as a dif­fi­cult col­lab­o­ra­tor.
“It taught me a very big les­son not only about music,” says Han­cock, “but about life.”
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

title: Christopher Hitchens Explains Why Homer’s Odyssey Still Matters to Our World (2000)
description:
in Uncategorized |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

At the moment, the answer to the ques­tion of why we should read Home­r’s Odyssey s
body:
in Uncategorized |   	July 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

At the moment, the answer to the ques­tion of why we should read Home­r’s Odyssey seems rather straight­for­ward: so we can more intel­li­gent­ly voice our opin­ions on Christo­pher Nolan’s new block­buster film adap­ta­tion. A quar­ter-cen­tu­ry ago, the mat­ter was some­what less clear. Still, an occa­sion had pre­sent­ed itself in the form of a new Eng­lish trans­la­tion, by Uni­ver­si­ty of Kansas clas­sics pro­fes­sor Stan­ley Lom­bar­do. That book, and the work of Homer in gen­er­al, was the sub­ject of a live two-hour round­table dis­cus­sion aired on C‑SPAN’s Book TV in the fall of 2000, which, with the Odyssey back in the zeit­geist, appeared on YouTube just days ago.
Apart from Lom­bar­do him­self, the par­tic­i­pants include Joseph Bot­tum, then lit­er­ary edi­tor of the Week­ly Stan­dard; jour­nal­ist and mil­i­tary vet­er­an Debra J. Dick­er­son; and Christo­pher Hitchens, who clear­ly par­tic­i­pat­ed not just because he hap­pened to be liv­ing in Wash­ing­ton, D.C., but also out of a gen­uine appre­ci­a­tion for the Odyssey and an under­stand­ing of its rel­e­vance in the mod­ern world. Ear­ly on in the text, he explains, Homer intro­duces the con­cepts of hubris and neme­sis, which “we can­not do with­out in ordi­nary dis­course. There are cer­tain pun­ish­ments that appear to fall on peo­ple, for orig­i­nal arro­gance or con­ceit, that we can’t con­ceive of relat­ing grand sto­ries with­out.”
There’s the “caprice of the gods,” with which every reli­gion has had to deal, as well as the even more uni­ver­sal feel­ing of nos­tal­gia, “a very overused and sen­ti­men­tal­ized term now, which lit­er­al­ly means — and can only real­ly mean — the yearn­ing to go home.” Adduc­ing such re-inter­pre­ta­tions by writ­ers from Alexan­der Pope to James Joyce, Hitchens declares that we think of the Odyssey as “the orig­i­nal nar­ra­tive of the striv­ing of human­i­ty — and of the need, also, to beware of what you want, in case you ever do, as Cavafy says, final­ly get home to Itha­ca. It may turn out that it’s bet­ter to trav­el hope­ful­ly than to arrive.”
The mat­ter of virtue also aris­es in the con­ver­sa­tion, and specif­i­cal­ly whether the range of virtues of which Homer sang (up to and includ­ing luck) would be rec­og­nized in our Chris­t­ian or post-Chris­t­ian world. To the avowed­ly athe­ist Hitchens’ mind, of course, we should already have been post-reli­gious. Home­r’s deities are “anthro­po­mor­phic gods; they are invent­ed by us, as all gods are.” But what­ev­er your reli­gion or lack there­of, “if you don’t know some­thing about clas­si­cal Greece, then you won’t be able, with much prof­it, to read Shake­speare, or Mil­ton, or Shel­ley, or Keats, or even Chaucer. It would be like not know­ing what the bible sto­ry was and then won­der­ing how you puz­zle your way through Shake­speare as well. It’s part of the under­lay; it’s part of the com­mon her­itage.” The trans­la­tions and re-inter­pre­ta­tions have kept com­ing, but Homer him­self still patient­ly awaits each of us.
Relat­ed con­tent:

title: How a 13th-Century Monk Created a Prayer Manuscript by Writing Over—and Accidentally Preserving—Archimedes’ Groundbreaking Mathematical Works
description:
in History, Math |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Ortho­dox monk named Johannes My
body:
in History, Math |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In Jerusalem of the year 1229, there lived a Greek Ortho­dox monk named Johannes Myronas. Need­ing some parch­ment for a prayer book, he grabbed some already-used pages, erased their exist­ing con­tent, and over them wrote down “prayers for the dead, prayers for repen­tance, bless­ings for the loaves at East­er, and even a prayer for those who were unrea­son­ably exclud­ed,” says math-and-sci­ence YouTu­ber Ben Syversen in the video above. Myronas may have ful­filled his reli­gious duty with­out using too much valu­able parch­ment, but he could­n’t have known the even greater rel­e­vance his actions would turn out to have had in the realm of math­e­mat­ics. For the pages he’d scrubbed were a Greek com­pi­la­tion con­tain­ing the only known copy of cer­tain works by the ancient poly­math Archimedes.
As it turns out, Myronas com­mit­ted per­haps the most notable act of inad­ver­tent preser­va­tion in the his­to­ry of math­e­mat­ics. We get the word palimpsest from the medieval prac­tice of over­writ­ing a page after first eras­ing what had been on it before, though incom­plete­ly; hence the mean­ing of mul­ti­ple lay­ers that have remained leg­i­ble over time.
In the case of what we now know as the Archimedes Palimpsest, that leg­i­bil­i­ty was achieved only with the aid of late twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry and ear­ly twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry tech­nol­o­gy, in addi­tion to the painstak­ing con­ser­va­tion effort required to keep this tenth-cen­tu­ry doc­u­ment in more or less one piece. (And all of that was only pos­si­ble thanks to the epic his­tor­i­cal jour­ney the Palimpsest took, which end­ed in 1998 when it sold for $2 mil­lion at Christie’s to a tech fig­ure we’re only assured is not Bill Gates.)


	

You can learn more about that project from the TED Talk just above by its direc­tor, the late William Noel of Bal­ti­more’s Wal­ters Art Muse­um. Thanks to his ded­i­ca­tion and that of his team, we now have writ­ings of Archimedes like the Stom­a­chion, which deals with a kind of chil­dren’s puz­zle that turns out to have con­sid­er­able sim­i­lar­i­ties with an ear­ly prob­lem in the field of com­bi­na­torics, and more impor­tant­ly, The Method of Mechan­i­cal The­o­rems, an expla­na­tion of cal­cu­lus-like pro­ce­dures for deter­min­ing area or vol­ume. None of this proves that Archimedes was the inven­tor of com­bi­na­torics or cal­cu­lus, exact­ly, but it does show us just how much fur­ther he’d man­aged to push Greek math­e­mat­ics than we’d pre­vi­ous­ly known. Besides, any work that can bring togeth­er his­to­ri­ans, clas­si­cists, math­e­mati­cians, con­ser­va­tors, physi­cists, and com­put­er sci­en­tists more than two mil­len­nia after its com­po­si­tion sure­ly mer­its a place in the canon.
Relat­ed con­tent:

title: Hear What Homer’s Odyssey Sounded Like When Sung in the Original Ancient Greek
description:
in History, Literature, Music |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
It’s been a human­ist tru­ism for some time
body:
in History, Literature, Music |   	July 29th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
It’s been a human­ist tru­ism for some time to say that Shake­speare speaks to every age, tran­scend­ing his time and place through the sheer force of his uni­ver­sal genius. But any hon­est stu­dent first encoun­ter­ing the plays will tell you dif­fer­ent­ly, as will many a sea­soned schol­ar who works hard to place the writer and his work in his­tor­i­cal con­text. Even one­time direc­tor of London’s Nation­al The­atre, Nicholas Hyt­ner, once said, “I’ll admit that I hard­ly ever go to a per­for­mance of one of Shakespeare’s plays with­out expe­ri­enc­ing blind pan­ic dur­ing the first five min­utes. I sit there think­ing… I have no idea what these peo­ple are talk­ing about.”
Of course, none of that means we can’t learn to appre­ci­ate Shake­speare, and we do not need a grad­u­ate-lev­el edu­ca­tion to do so. But much of his archa­ic lan­guage and obscure ref­er­ences will always sound for­eign to mod­ern ears. How much more so, then, the lan­guage of the ancient Greeks, whether in trans­la­tion or not? Although we’ve also been taught to think of the Home­r­ic epics as con­tain­ers of uni­ver­sal truth and beau­ty, the world of Homer was, in many ways, an alien one—and the lit­er­a­ture of ancient Greece was far clos­er to song than even Shakespeare’s musi­cal speech­es.
In fact, “before writ­ing was gen­er­al­ly known among the Greeks,” the Uni­ver­si­ty of Cincin­nati notes, “poets recit­ed and sang sto­ries for audi­ences at the courts of city lead­ers and at fes­ti­vals. A poet could actu­al­ly impro­vise a tale in the six-beat rhythm of Greek verse if he knew the plot of his sto­ry.” We do not know whether Homer was one enter­pris­ing scribe or “a group of poets whose works on the theme of Troy were col­lect­ed” under one name. But in either case, that poet or poets heard the tales of Hec­tor and Achilles, Odysseus and Pene­lope, and all those med­dling gods sung before they wrote them down. Now, thanks to Georg Danek of the Uni­ver­si­ty of Vien­na and Ste­fan Hagel of the Aus­tri­an Acad­e­my of Sci­ences, we have some idea of what those songs may have sound­ed like.
“In the course of the last years,” write Danek and Hagel, “we have devel­oped a tech­nique of singing the Home­r­ic epics, which is appro­pri­ate for the pri­mar­i­ly oral tra­di­tion from which these poems emerge.” The two schol­ars cau­tion that their the­o­ret­i­cal recre­ations are “not to be under­stood as the exact recon­struc­tion of a giv­en melody, but as an approach to the tech­nique the Home­r­ic singers used to accom­mo­date melod­ic prin­ci­ples to the demands of the indi­vid­ual verse.” Accom­pa­nied by a four-stringed lyre-like instru­ment called a phorminx, “the Home­r­ic bard” would impro­vise the “melody at the same time as he impro­vised his text, which was unique in every per­for­mance.” In the audio above, you can hear Danek and Hagel’s melod­ic recre­ation of lines 267–366 of book 8 of the Odyssey, in which Demod­ocus sings about the love of Ares and Aphrodite.
At their site, the two schol­ars present an abstract of their Home­r­ic singing the­o­ry, with musi­co­log­i­cal and lin­guis­tic evi­dence for the recre­ation. Their tech­ni­cal cri­te­ria will con­fuse the non-spe­cial­ist, and none but ancient Greek speak­ers will under­stand the record­ing above. But it brings us a lit­tle clos­er to expe­ri­enc­ing Home­r’s epic poet­ry, “the foun­da­tion stones of Euro­pean Lit­er­a­ture,” as the ancient Greeks might have expe­ri­enced it.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: Nature or Culture? Europeans Can Vote on the New Banknote Design
description: What best represents European life? The eternal dichotomy of nature vs. culture structures the Central Bank’s quest for a new banknote design, and
body:
What best represents European life? The eternal dichotomy of nature vs. culture structures the Central Bank’s quest for a new banknote design, and now, the public can vote and offer feedback on ten proposals. 
A panel of jurors selected the designs, which follow one of two themes: European places and ideas or birds and rivers, the latter of which is meant to symbolize freedom and unity. While the basic elements are the same—all collections devoted to culture feature the same six figures, including Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci, composer Ludwig van Beethoven, scientist Marie Curie, opera singer Maria Callas, and authors Bertha von Suttner and Miguel de Cervantes, for example—individual approaches appear in the layout, aesthetic, and composition.
Voting is open through mid-September, when jurors will select one design that will go through an additional vetting process before the organization adopts it entirely. View all ten on the bank’s website.

title: 'Colorstruck!' Examines the Connection Between Race and Chromatic Expression
description: A nude Black woman lies on a stark white chaise, her head propped up by her thin arm. She’s surrounded by flat, abstracted color in the form of fr
body:
A nude Black woman lies on a stark white chaise, her head propped up by her thin arm. She’s surrounded by flat, abstracted color in the form of fruits and fabrics, and a glass coupe and bottle on a nearby table offer a clear, rather than refracted, view of the vibrant scene. Rendered in oil on burlap, the painting by William H. Johnson is commanding in its palette and subject matter and an exemplary work in a new book by art historian Richard J. Powell.
Forthcoming this fall from Princeton University Press, Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect delves into the ways that color and social, political, and cultural forces intersect in Black American art. Powell takes an expansive approach to each of the three topics—painting, pigment, and affect—and examines works by a wide group of artists, including Jacob Lawrence, Alma Thomas, Lorna Simpson, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Nina Chanel Abney. His interest is in the dynamic interplay of paint and pigment and what the two reveal about both the artists and the viewers.
William H. Johnson, “Nude” (c. 1939), oil on burlap, 29 ¾ x 38 ¼ inches. Image courtesy of Smithsonian American Art Museum and Art Resource
Sharing a root with words like awestruck or starstruck, colorstruck is a slang term that evolved from “a Black person who preferred associating with light-skinned Blacks or White people to anyone inordinately preoccupied with race,” Powell writes. The idea is largely associated with colorism, although in his view, it can also be applied to the ways we marvel at and can even be overwhelmingly affected by an artist’s palette. He adds: 

What if a painter, like early Black modernist Willian H. Johnson, set aside the more pejorative insinuations in the idea of being colorstruck, and instead used the paint medium, an intense color palette, racial Blackness, and most important, his abstracting inclinations to produce an expressionistic, evocative, and disruptive work of art? 

The book continues in this line of thinking as it connects what is often thought of as a universal concept—that color exists, and humans respond to certain hues in particular ways—and the distinct context of race in America. Richly illustrated with archival photographs and numerous artworks, the volume captures the relationship between the unique experience of an artist and her viewer and the broader powers that inform those dynamics.
Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect will be published in September, and you can pre-order your copy through Bookshop.
Hervé Télémaque, “Négrerie (Black cultural effects)” (1974), lithograph, 30 x 22 inches. Image © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource
Alma Thomas, “The Eclipse” (1970), acrylic on canvas, 62 x 49 ¾ inches. Image courtesy of Smithsonian American Art Museum and Art Resource
Malcolm Bailey, “Untitled” (1972), cut and pasted paper and acrylic on Plexiglas, 36 x 36 inches. Image copyright © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource
Charles Alston, “Girl in a Red Dress” (1934), oil on canvas, 28 x 22 inches. Image © The Metropolitan Museum of Art, courtesy of Art Resource

title: Dynamic Scenes Emerge from Fumiaki Aono's Wooden Assemblages
description: Since 1998, Fumiaki Aono has been interested in how objects circulate and what happens when they appear in new contexts. Questions of restoration
body:
Since 1998, Fumiaki Aono has been interested in how objects circulate and what happens when they appear in new contexts. Questions of restoration and regeneration naturally followed, and wood became a prime medium for exploring these themes.
Today, Aono continues to revitalize found objects, particularly discarded furniture. Dressers, chests, and cabinets stack into towering assemblages and become the imaginative backdrop for the artist’s constructed scenes. Converted drawers appear like apartment buildings on a summer day, with tenants leaning out windows and hanging out at street level. Several works also depict box trucks and other vehicles emerging from wooden furnishings, while bicycles, hats, and shoes jut from the edges of sculptures to convey a sense of movement and evolution.

After experimenting with plywood and timber, Aono’s transition to secondhand furniture added a conceptual layer to the pieces. These objects “brought the old memories and lived histories of people into the imagery of the work. In recent years, my concept of ‘regeneration’ has evolved beyond mere physical form; it has become a highly complex and multifaceted process encompassing history, memory, ancient legends, and the deep psyche,” he says.
Explore more from the artist on his website and Instagram.
